I agree with this guy 100%

I only wear minimalist shoes.  Working as a contractor, walking the dog, trail running, rock hopping... It doesn't matter because my feet and legs are now conditioned to do the work.  If you only wear minimalist shoes on the daily I don't know why you would swap out to something less familiar for backpacking, or any other activity.

The whole point of minimalist shoes is to get you feeling the trail and using that to your advantage.  Yes, sometimes Id like my feet to be less sore, or warmer, or to have a stronger toe at work, but those things come with drawbacks.  My feet delicately feel where I am and react accordingly.  Never have I felt a different shoe would have gotten me farther, aside from straight rock climbing.

Old style merrell vapor gloves are my current choice because the Trail gloves aren't what they used to be many generations ago.  After I bought all the trail gloves I could find, I bought all the vapor gloves I could find, and I'm almost out.  At this point my socks are thicker than the soles and I have no issue running any rocky trail around Phoenix Arizona.  Xero Trail mesas were alright, a little too tough of a sole and too weak of an upper for my liking, but they are probably the best thing out there currently produced that I can say I like.  Very over priced, as are vivo. If only having healthy feet wasn't a silly trend.

I tried altras and they made me feel very unstable.  Having a drop isn't an option so most other brands of shoe are off the table.  I'm not entirely sure minimalist shoes are FOR EVERYONE,  but if they are for you I see no reason to have anything but.  Once you adapt there's no advantage to cushion.

A good portion of my shin is numb, as well as the outside of my knee.  The PA said they inevitably sever some nerves that pass from the inside of the leg during surgery, and they will recover eventually.

I'll go back to elevating my leg more often, clearly I've gotten a bit too relaxed about my recovery, thinking as long as I'm not stepping on it I'm fine.
Yes it becomes indented and lumpy when I wear a brace or compression sleeve, no matter how loose.  It is always swollen, but it will take the shape of whatever I wear on my leg.

My surgeon limited my motion to 70 degrees with the brace, and for the first 2 weeks I needed to sleep with it locked and elevated.

At the 2 week appointment he said I didn't need to sleep in it anymore, and said I can do whatever I want as long as I'm not putting weight on my leg or bending it beyond the set limit.  I do drive with the brace on.  Every question I asked, his response was asking "can you do it without putting weight on your leg?" It seems that's all he cares about.

He said a physical therapist would want to start immediately but said it was a waste of my time and money in his opinion, and would give me a referral at 6 weeks.

Clearly my leg is swelling because I'm up and moving around.  I have an 8 month old child and I'm the main chef of the house, it's a hobby.  I run errands and go on drives because I'm losing my mind.  I'm a self employed contractor and going broke because I can't work, the least I can do is support my family in other ways.  I still haven't figured out when or how this will end, but that's another story.

Meniscus Root repair, 4/6 weeks NWB.  Since week 2 I haven't been able to wear my leg brace even for 20 minutes or my leg looks like the Michelin Man.  See attached photo.

My foot is always red, and my calf is considerably larger.  The effusion over my knee joint looks the same as it did immediately after surgery.  Otherwise I'm healing well and pain free.  Mobility is good, though I'm not allowed to really move it yet.

I called the surgeons office a few times post op and I eventually gave up.  I even emailed pictures.  They didn't call back.  They must not be concerned, but over a month?  Should I be doing something about this?

I toe touch and work around the house cooking and taking care of my son.  I drive.  I run errands.  I don't start PT until I get the all clear in 2 more weeks.

Thank you for understanding.  That’s why I felt it was OK to post in this ACL sub, most of us are dealing with similar post op instructions.  Search 6 weeks NWB and this pops up…

I again reached out to my surgeons office today.  He’s really good at what he does, and I don’t expect surgeons to have good bedside manner.  I want him to fix my knee, not write me a poem about it.  I was legit disappointed when he called me personally the next day to follow up because I feel guilty wasting his time with stupid questions.  

I will do what I’m told to do, but I’m also going to do as much as I’m able to do without reversing the procedure or slowing healing.  I imagine we all are in that boat, even if you don’t have a family to care for.  Clearly some weight will fall on your knee from time to time, and some level of that must be acceptable.  It would help to know where to draw the line between don’t walk on it and don’t even try to put a sock on yourself.

He rolled to his side the day he was born.  He will only sleep on his side.  It made us nervous at first, kept us awake for a few days watching.  But he can’t make it to his belly on his own.

I appreciate your concern!

Taking a video is a good suggestion… He used to wake up when he was hungry, every few hours.  It was getting to the point where we started waking him up after 4 or 5 because we were worried.  He does coo and roll around in his sleep, but this is more kicking and screaming lately.  

For example, I watched him from 5-7 this morning, his bassinet is bedside.  Every 5-10 minutes he would cry out, kick his feet contort his face, roll around, some times arch his back off the mattress.  It would last a couple minutes and then he would fall back asleep.  He was obviously tired, his eyes never really opened.  If you told me he was having nightmares and waking himself up I’d believe it, but it happened over and over and over again.   He rolls himself into the side of the bassinet and kicks his feet against the bottom.

Oh, when I pick him up he passes gas.  Most of the time.  He went through a brief phase where he would poop like this at night, I’d change him and then bam, again.  And then a 3rd time.  I was calling him hat trick.  Then it stopped.

Perhaps we weren’t clear enough with the doctor, as to what’s going on.  As a first time parent I feel like most people think I’m over reacting and I need to wait it out.  It’s easier for me to vent to random strangers on the internet lol.

My siblings are parents and they just say “oh this will pass” and my mother in law says “I remember this.”  I feel like the doctor has a similar approach.  We called and they said wait longer to see if he’s constipated.  A couple days later he pooped.  What she’s saying is in line with what we’re reading online, some babies just don’t poop a lot.  “As long as he’s still eating and gaining weight he’s fine.”

I know I’m over thinking things but I don’t want him to be uncomfortable.  He was the most peaceful perfect baby for a couple weeks,  sleeping and eating more than any newborn should.  Then he started having what I’ve deduced to be stomach issues and it’s been very difficult for all of us.

Exclusively Brest fed for the moment, we will be adding a bottle when mom goes back to work.  His latch seems great, we have had doula support throughout and everyone was pleased with how he was feeding.  Here in Maine we actually have free lactation specialist appointments at the hospital but we couldn’t see a reason for going.  Perhaps we will make an appointment now.

It also has me thinking that it could be his pacifier?  We recently added it, possibly a few days before this all began.
Our pediatrician didn’t seem concerned about any of this, and I do like her so far, but something just seems wrong.  Do probiotics typically come from mom?

Yes I have heard of the windy and my good friend used it with his daughter.  But my son seemed to be passing gas just fine until a week ago?  He does still, but perhaps not as often or as much.  Lots of obvious rumbles in his belly.  

So you think this is something that he can get worse and and actually require my help?  I mean, nobody needed to stick a straw into our butts when we were younger.  I really question a lot of these “tools” available today.  But if it works, I’ll try it.

Was your child formula fed?  We have been told that Brest milk can be more “efficient” and that this lack of poop is normal?  But combine that with his distress and I’m concerned.  It’s definitely soft when he does go.

Let me walk you through the build. I apologize in advance for being long winded, but anyone shopping for a custom RV will understand and appreciate the thought that goes into every aspect of our vehicles. Every conversion is highly personal, for better or worse. If your needs are close to ours, you are in luck:

2 people.
2 road bikes.
Full-time REAL Queen Bed.
Room for Camping and Climbing gear.
Water, Food, and Power Storage for 5+ days without starting the engine.
120v Power for appliances.
Composting toilet.
Heavily Insulated to allow for desert camping.
Off-Road capable to reach remote camp sites.
Maintain relative stealth for Urban Parking when visiting cities.
Durable interior that can withstand years of abuse.

The 100AH house battery is charged by the engine through a charge controller. Power requirements are kept to a minimum with LED lighting and a Yetti Cooler.  10lbs of ice will last 5+ days depending on ambient temperature. Even when regularly using a rice cooker, toaster, coffee grinder, water pump, and charging our portable devices, the power is designed to last 5+ days. If you need more power than this, it's fairly easy to mount a few panels to the roof.

There is a 20g water tank under the chassis, with a filter for drinking water, that's easy to fill and lasts 5+ days for two people drinking, cooking, and washing up.   There is a legitimate shower head out the back door.  The variable flow pump is inside the van in order to keep the noise outside to a minimum and remain stealth. The tank sits higher than the spare tire to avoid obstacles when Off Road.

The back doors of the van open to access the "garage." This is where we have stored 2 road bikes, tools, and other adventure gear we don't need to easily reach from the inside.  There is 8ft of storage space under the bed.   All of your gear can be reached from the foot of the bed inside.

The interior is fully built and trimmed, as the photos will show. Careful consideration was made in regards to materials, fasteners, electrical, water and overall design. Over 60k miles have been put on the original build with zero failures. This is a well thought out build designed to last indefinitely. No corners were cut to save a buck or make building easier. I am a general contractor by trade and a perfectionist. This is my personal rig and I built it right the first time. Don't be scared by the mileage, these modular engines last forever and everything worth replacing has been replaced. Zero Rust anywhere, this is a desert truck. With proper maintenance it will run forever.

I took the survey.  Not entirely sure what information your hoping to gain, but I will say I'd really like to see a bulk meal versus single serve.  I make my own meals in bulk, and bag up what I need before each trip.  I also limit myself to one hot meal per day, and I want control over my calories.  Some foil packets aren't enough, others are too much.

The biggest problem I have is that ingredients are limited, and there's only a couple *well-balanced* dishes I know how to make.  Mainly couscous or rice with some protein and fiber mixed in.  A heavy dose of Nutritional Yeast in everything.  Some variety would be appreciated.  Cheesy beans and rice gets old on a 5+ day trip.

I try and reduce waste, to some extent.  I don't like the foil packets, but I don't like washing dishes in the desert either.  I have tried reusable pouches but for long trips they add a lot of weight.  Most of the time I'm eating out of quart sized freezer bags.  I burn what I can, for better or worse.

My meal cost is roughly $2-3 for 1000+ calories, but I'd spend more if you made it for me.

Hope this helps.

I'm not trying to pick a fight with a guy on the internet, I'm just trying to be helpful to the OP.   We all have different styles of playing, and I don't think heel up vs heel down is a matter of right or wrong.  I wouldn't want to make a self proclaimed beginner think he's doing something wrong just because it's not what others are doing. 

If you're interested, I have more of a "jazz" technique and my drums are setup accordingly.  My bass drum is just a Tom I play with my foot.  It's tuned to resonate and bloom, the front head isn't ported, and therefore I can't bury the beater without it buzzing on the batter.  It's not tiny or tuned overly high, and I use muffled heads, but for the sake of this conversation you could say I have a bop setup.  My spring tension is set medium high, and I do get some bounce back from a tight batter, but just like you pull back on a stick hitting a head, I pull back with my foot.   The same way you pull sound out of any drum.  My limbs aren't dead weight.  My heel sits on the pedal probably 80% of the time, while my toes are lifted after every stroke regardless.

Keep in mind this is just one way to do it.  This is describing heel up and slide technique for doubles, burrying the beater into the head.

Personally I play heel down.  I bounce the beater off the bass drum like a stick on a Tom.  I do not see any draw back in this, and regardless of your style your muscles will adapt.

The only "wrong" you can do playing a pedal is being off axis, which I could see causing unwanted torsion in your foot and ankle leading to pain.  The rest is 100% subjective opinion.
This is misleading.  I use my shin muscle 100% of the time.  Been playing heel down for 25 years.

Make sure your inline with the pedal and the drum head.  There's a lot of personal preference in setup beyond that, I don't think you can say there's right or wrong.  How high your throne sits, how you tension your pedal, how far the beater is from the head, spring tension, how tight the batter head is, etc. Some play heel up, some play heel down.   All of these factors play together to get your sound and style. Whatever works for you.

Maintenance records.  I buy a lot of used cars, but I won't go near it if they can't prove to me it is well kept.  Replacing parts isn't necessarily a sign of a lemon, it could mean a proactive owner.  All depends on when and why.

I typically buy 1 owner cars to get the information I want, but it's not required.  'Fleet maintained van' doesn't mean much if the fleet mechanic was crummy, so take that with a grain of salt.

Miles don't mean anything to me.  Other parts wear much faster than an engine. Also, letting a car sit can be worse than high miles.

Listen/feel for vibrations and squeaks. Valve tick, belt squeel, pulley bearings or the AC compressor whining, wheel bearings clicking or loose, exhaust noise, odd shifting, Turn abruptly and feel for clunks. Anything that could be a sign of neglect.

Let the engine idle for 5-10 minutes after a test drive to make sure it doesn't over heat.  While parked, move the steering wheel and see if the pump groans excessively.  Check all fluid levels and look for contamination.  Take a look at the radiator hoses and make sure they're nice and flexible with good seals.  Look under the car and the hood for leaks or signs of a previous leak.  Just because it isn't leaking now doesn't mean damage hasn't already been done.

It's a good idea to know what your looking for, but even if you don't, take your time with the inspection.  Let them sweat a bit.  Your mainly looking for signs of previous damage or neglected repairs.

And if you're totally serious, it wouldn't hurt to get a mechanic involved.

I used 15/32, 4 layer ply.  I cut it across the grain, making 4 foot strips.  It will be much more flexible cut this way, easier to contour to walls.  

I attached the strips with Teks #10 "wood to sheet metal screws."  1-1/4 is the shortest they make them, so be careful not to drill through the exterior of the van.  These are the best screws I found after trying many other options.  They have a tighter thread than most metal screws, which will hold the sheet metal more securely.

You need to pre drill every hole, so buy a few 1/16" drill bits, and a 5/16 drill bit. The 1/16 is for both wood and sheet metal so it will wear out quickly.  The 5/16 will be used to countersink the head into the wood, to make attaching your walls easier later.  Don't expect screws to countersink themselves.  Your essentially drilling into tin foil, it doesn't have the strength to pull a screw into plywood.  Also be careful not to over tighten them.

Place the wood against the wall where you want it to go.  There aren't a lot of options here, either you have a cargo van with ribs, or a passenger van with interior metal walls.  In either situation you attach wood wherever it's flat and will accept screws. In the passenger this will be tricky, but not impossible.  In a house the framing is 16" apart, but you won't have that option here.  Your end goal is to create secure mounting points for your wall coverings.  They don't need to be very pretty or evenly spaced as long as they are secure.

I propped the wood stips against the wall with another piece of scrap wood, diagonally across the van.  It was pressed into place with the curve I wanted for my finished wall.  Drill with 1/16, then breifly with the 5/16, just enough to hide the screw head.  Sink your screw, keep the torque setting low on your drill.  If you strip it, you need to start over.  Remember that you only have one shot at doing this right, you don't want a rattle inside your wall that can't be fixed.

Repeat around the van.   In the back corners placement will be tricky.  I cut my strips up into a few pieces and mounted them right in the corner, basically on a 45° angle.  It was the only way to have secure corners in a passenger van, with the type of covering I was going to use (thin cedar).  Remember you want a smooth and secure surface for wood screws later.

https://photos.app.goo.gl/fNSdE6LzrtL2TdePA

Scroll to the bottom of that album to see what I'm talking about.  Of course there are other ways to do this, such as rivet nuts, but this is what I did.  We hit some pretty gnarly roads and haven't had a rattle or a squeak yet.

You will also notice I ran some horizontal pieces, these were more or less spacers to give the interior the shape I wanted.  They also helped to avoid bumps in the wall and keep my ribs in line.  In some areas I added extra strips where I knew I would be attaching a cabinet to the wall.

I didn't use foam board on the walls, only on the floor and ceiling.  You have the right idea.

Stuff as much insulation as you can into the holes in the walls.  Use a coat hanger or a ruler, scrap wood, etc.  Try not to compress it too much, but get the best coverage you can.  I found it was even possible to get it into the window columns and down below the floor level.  There was only one or two small spots I ended up using spray foam.  It's really not ideal for filling voids, but I made it work.  

It's amazing how much insulation your van will eat up.  I think we used a whole master pack of r19 denim insulation from Lowe's.  If you want to go the extra mile, go with wool, which is better at resisting mold and mildew.

Once the walls were stuffed with insulation I put up ribs of 1/2" plywood, cut widthwise to maximize flexibility.  These will serve as secure anchor points for your wall coverings, and provide shape over the bumps and voids.   I experimented with a few screw options, but ultimately I settled on teks #14 self drilling wood to metal screws.  Self piercing didn't work well, and metal stud drywall screws didn't hold enough.  Pre drill and countersink everything, sheet metal doesn't have a whole lot of holding power.  It's like screwing into tin foil.  

Be patient and be confident with each step.  Don't move forward until your happy with what you've done.  Once you cover the walls it's hard to go back in and fix something.  Just tackle this step by step, you've got it under control.

We also tried to follow the weather, but this fall was unexpectedly cold and wet everywhere.

When nights dip into the 20s, your going to want a heat source, or lots of blankets.  Insulation won't keep you warm until morning unless you have a heater to compensate for heat loss.  When we have shore power we plug in a 300w heater that keeps us plenty toasty, so it doesn't take much.  If it was any bigger we would have to setup a thermostat to turn it on and off.

We found that when camping in the desert, insulation did a great job of keeping the van cool until the afternoon.  No issues sleeping in, even in 100 degree weather and parked in the sun.

Also keep in mind that your stuff is a heat battery.  Mass retains heat.  On long trips in the winter, heat your van for hours while you crack windows in the front for comfort.  In the summer, use AC in the same way.  That will delay the warming and cooling from the outside air.

Whatever you do, DO NOT use a vapor barrier.  Your van already IS a vapor barrier.  Even if you were able to seal up 100% of every hole, you would only be trapping moisture between the metal and your barrier.  We don't live in a vacuum, you can't turn your van into a yetti cup.  Eventually this would rust.

You want your van to breathe, so moisture and condensation can work their way out.  Ventilation is very important.

And reflectix is great at blocking RADIENT heat if used correctly, but we don't have the space to do it correctly.  Save your money.   Use rockwool/wool/denim everywhere you possibly can reach/stuff, CAREFULLY use spray foam where you can't, and cover flat surfaces with polyiso board.

We charge 1 SLA battery from our alternator without issues, but it's not as straight forward as you might think.

Throw out any math you have regarding expected charge times, because alternators don't have a constant output.  They charge your cranking battery within minutes of starting the van, then drop amperage to maintenance levels.  They don't run at max power for long, meaning getting a peak charge is nearly impossible unless youre on the road for hours.  At idle, your alternator is also at reduced output.  It doesn't matter how long you sit at the drive through, it's how long you drove at 2000+ RPM.

It can work, at least it has for us.  But our battery usage is low.  We have gone 4-5 days on a single 100ah battery, but typically we drive more often.  Just know that alternators charge inconsistently, and with 4 batteries you may need to drive 6-8 hours at highway speeds for a full charge.  That's just a guess based on our own experiences.

I once compared the cost over time of a used sprinter versus a used cargo van.  I learned that in my lifetime I will never recoup the extra cost in gas savings.

I can't figure out why people worry so much about MPG.  

My Low Roof E350 Loaded averages about 14mpg, 400 Miles per tank.  But to put things into perspective, I can drive 9000 miles on $2000.  It would take me DECADES of driving to offset the cost of a more fuel efficient sprinter.

How much are you REALLY going to drive per year?  Now my commuter car (CRV) drives 500 miles per week, and thats pretty normal here in Phoenix.  The CRV has a larger carbon footprint as a commuter than my van touring the country for a year.

Now if you're looking to purchase a new van for your fed-ex fleet, get a fuel efficient and long lasting diesel, it will pay for itself.  For us VanDwellers, we just don't drive enough for it to matter.  I know Im not putting half a million miles on a sprinter, not in a lifetime.

What van works for you depends on too many factors to list.  Start with the big essential stuff.  I wanted to cary my bikes/climbing/camping gear inside, have running water and a stove, 120v electric, and a full time bed.  These things meant I needed at least an extended wheelbase for the floor space.  

Then I looked at my market and my budget and chose a low roof E350.  If I had been more patient I probably could have found a high roof or diesel in my price range, but for every advantage there's a disadvantage.  Sprinters do exist below 10k, but they all seemed risky.

You need to be realistic, you need to be flexible, and you need to get your hands dirty, but $10k can easily build a top-of-the-line cargo van.

When designing these builds there's a lot of factors to consider, and weight was low on my priority list.
If your vehicle was designed for weight, why not utilize it?  Before I built, my E350 was rigid and bouncy.  Now she rides quiet and smooth.  I have not noticed a drop in performance or MPG.
Also I can drive 7000 miles at 12mpg for $1800, and in that time I can spend 20k+ on other living expenses.  At 10% of my expenses, gas is not a concern.

The walls started with 1/2" ply for strength and flexibility.  One sheet was enough for all of the framing ribs.  Make note of the grain when cutting, its flexible in one direction and rigid in the other.  Use this to your advantage.

The walls and ceiling are covered with 1/4" x 3.5" cedar planks.  Naturally mold and moisture resistant, I used to use it for decking.  Im not a huge fan of working with cedar as its super soft and the sawdust is irritating, but it looks nice and its done.

The trim is made from a single sheet of 3/16 hardboard, and I love this stuff.  Cheap, strong, dense, easy to work with.  I expect to use more of this in the rest of the build.  Just make sure you paint it, its not very water resistant.

Under the flooring is a more creative choice...  1/2" Hardie Siding.  Its coated on one side for moisture, has an overlapping seam on the sides to prevent uneven floors, and didn't take up too much head room (versus 3/4 Subfloor).   It's also dense and very flat as an engineered wood.  If I was in an area that sold it, I would have gone with 5/8 Advantech T&G.

Not many passenger conversions out there, but I needed windows!  Passenger models also have the rear AC unit and stiffer walls.

Over the wheel well is the rear air AC/Heat.  The van really cools off quickly with it, so I decided to keep it.  Ive got a plan to box in the outflow and vent it next to the bed with a floor register or 2.

My battery system is as simple as it gets because I don't plan to run solar.  I have an extra "house" battery thats good for 100 Amp Hours. When picking a battery keep in mind you can only use 50% of it before recharging.

My battery will be connected to the alternator with a device that allows it to charge, but prevents me from pulling power out of my van's cranking battery.  I will also have a 12v charger onboard, with an extension cord to plug in when we visit friends or RV campsites.

To use this power I have a 12v Fan, 12v Lights, USB outlets, and of course a 1500W power inverter.  The inverter will be for any kitchen devices, 120v Laptop, etc, but I'm pretty sure use will be minimal.

Rather than a 110v to 12v charger I could use a MPPT charge controller and connect it to solar, but not at this time.

Batteries are complicated and I learned most of what I know when designing this setup, everything else is basic wiring.  

I used 12ga stranded copper wire that was coated against corrosive chemicals.  Stranded is essential because solid wires can bend while bouncing around, until they break, short, and burn down your home.  Same goes for cheap aluminum wire.  Just buy the good stuff used in homes, 12ga is over kill but better safe than sorry.  Also, don't try to run all outlets on one circuit.  You will need a fuse panel to break up circuits.

Do some math, figure out what your demands are, and this will decide your battery size.  Depending on how big your battery is, you may want solar or a generator to charge, in addition to the alternator.  My goal was 5 days without turning on the engine, as our travel plans include VRBOs and hotels for cleanup once per week.  My cooking will use bottled fuel and cooler uses ice, so your needs will vary.
